references.text: Abram goes down to Egypt because of a famine, which mirrors Jacob's decision to send his sons to Egypt to buy grain.
Isaac goes to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar because of a famine, parallel to Jacob's action of sending his sons to Egypt to survive the famine.
Describes the famine that affected the whole world and led people from all nations to come to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain, directly related to why Jacob sends his sons to Egypt.
Stephen refers to the famine that brought Jacob's family to Egypt, highlighting the importance of this event in Israel's history.
Judah tells his father they must go to buy food so that they may live and not die—the same expression and motivation as in 42:2.
Uses an identical formula ('live and not die') to show a theological parallel: from the family's search for food to the entire nation's struggle for survival.
Creates a theological contrast between Egypt as God's solution to famine (Gen) and Egypt as a forbidden refuge (Jer), illuminating the people's trust in God.
New Testament allusion that confirms the event and places it within God's overarching plan of salvation (Stephen's speech).
